issues.issue: The notice states coverage is limited to claims 'REPORTED TO THE INSURER, IN WRITING, DURING THE POLICY PERIOD', while Insuring Agreement I.A. and Section VIII.B. allow a claim to be reported during an 'extended reporting period' and deem it made on the last day of the policy period. The two statements of the reporting deadline cannot be read together without qualification.

The Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 exceeds the Total Policy Aggregate of $7,000,000 stated in Item 4., yet Section II.D. calls Item 2.c. 'the maximum liability of the Insurer pursuant to this Policy'. A court would have to decide which aggregate governs Coverage A losses.

Item 3.c. sets a $5,000,000 Coverage B aggregate that Section II.F. calls 'the maximum liability of the Insurer pursuant to this Policy', while Item 4. sets a $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate said in II.G. to be the maximum for all coverages. The relationship between the two aggregates is left circular by the 'subject to' cross-references.

The $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate is smaller than the $9,000,000 Coverage A aggregate in Item 2.c., and Section II.G. makes it 'subject to' Subsections C.-F. which in turn make Items 2.c. and 3.c. the maximum. Which figure caps the Insurer's exposure is genuinely unresolved on the face of the instrument.

Item 5. deems the premium '100 % minimum-earned as of the first day of the Policy Period', but General Condition IX.A.3. contemplates 'remaining unearned premium' earned pro rata and a refund of unearned premium within thirty days of cancellation. If the whole premium is minimum-earned at inception there can never be unearned premium to refund.

Item 8. designates covered locations by reference to Endorsements 5 and 11, but Endorsement 11 schedules 'non-owned covered locations' which its own amended definition of 'covered location' treats as a separate category. Whether the Endorsement 11 sites are Item 8. 'covered locations' is left open.

The preamble limits coverage to claims 'REPORTED TO THE INSURER, IN WRITING, DURING THE POLICY PERIOD', while Insuring Agreement I.A. and Section VIII. permit reporting during an 'extended reporting period'. The absolute preamble and the qualified operative text point in different directions.

The convention says quoted words are 'defined in Section V., DEFINITIONS', yet endorsements introduce quoted defined terms elsewhere and Endorsement 6 uses the quoted term 'covered operations' which is defined nowhere. The convention cannot be applied to every quoted term in the instrument.

Insuring Agreement I.A. is 'deleted in its entirety and replaced' twice over — once by Endorsement 5 (adding retroactive-date coverage for scheduled sites) and again by Endorsement 10 (adding transportation and omitting the retroactive-date option). Which replacement text governs Coverage A is unresolved.

The grant covers only 'pollution conditions' that 'first commence, in their entirety, during the policy period', a phrase that gives no rule for a condition that develops or continues across periods. 'In their entirety' is capable of more than one reading.

Coverage B insures conditions that 'first commenced, in whole or part, prior to the policy period', while Exclusion VI.K. removes pollution conditions in existence and reported to a 'responsible person' prior to the policy period. The reach of Coverage B is therefore defined largely by an exclusion that cuts against it.

A single retention applies to all costs arising out of the 'same, continuous, repeated, or related' pollution condition, and 'related' is undefined and notoriously elastic. Whether separate outbreaks at separate scheduled locations are 'related' turns entirely on that word.

The per-condition limit aggregates everything arising out of the 'same, continuous, repeated, or related' pollution condition, and 'related' is left undefined with no test of relatedness. Whether multiple contaminations are one condition or many is decided by that undefined word.

II.D. calls Item 2.c. ($9,000,000) 'the maximum liability of the Insurer pursuant to this Policy', while II.G. calls Item 4. ($7,000,000) the maximum liability for all coverages. The two 'maximum liability' statements cannot both be literally true.
The limit turns on the 'same, continuous, repeated, or related' pollution condition without any definition of 'related'. That word alone determines whether one or several per-condition limits apply.

II.F. states Item 3.c. is 'the maximum liability of the Insurer pursuant to this Policy' while II.G. gives that role to the smaller Total Policy Aggregate in Item 4. The competing 'maximum liability' statements require reconciliation.

II.G. makes the Total Policy Aggregate 'subject to' Subsections C., D., E. and F., but D. and F. themselves declare the larger coverage-specific aggregates to be the Insurer's maximum liability, producing a circular hierarchy. With Item 2.c. at $9,000,000 and Item 4. at $7,000,000 the circularity has real money behind it.

The deeming provision turns on 'continuous, repeated, or related' pollution conditions and then declares that 'no other policy shall respond', purporting to govern instruments not before the court. Both the relatedness test and the reach of that last clause are open to argument.

Section III.A. is deleted and replaced in its entirety by Endorsement 6, II.A., which ends the defense duty on exhaustion of the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit as well; the original text survives in the printed policy. A reader is left with two defense-duty provisions in the same instrument.

The Insurer 'shall have the right to select legal counsel' but selection 'shall not be done without the consent of the insured', leaving it unclear who ultimately controls the choice. The provision then denies coverage for defense costs incurred before that selection, without a time limit on when the Insurer must select.

Section III.C. is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 4, III.C., yet the original remains printed in the policy form. The instrument contains two versions of the same consultant-retention condition.

Section III.D. is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6, II.D., which instead erodes the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate. The original and replacement erosion rules sit side by side in the instrument.

The Insurer's defense duty ends only if the recommended settlement 'does not impose any additional unreasonable burdens on the insured', a standard the provision does not define or measure. Whether a proposed settlement imposes such a burden is exactly the sort of question a court is asked to construe.

Coverage is limited to pollution conditions 'located' in the United States, but the insuring agreements cover conditions 'migrating from' a covered location, leaving migration across a border unaddressed. 'Located' has no fixed referent for a moving condition.

The US-only territory sits against the definitions of 'environmental law' and 'government action', which expressly reach 'provincial' law, and against Endorsement 15's provision for service of suit by a Canadian resident insured. The instrument both confines and contemplates coverage beyond the United States.

'Claim' requires a 'written assertion of a legal right received by the insured from a third-party', and whether a regulatory directive, quarantine order or depopulation notice is such an assertion is genuinely arguable. The 'including, but not limited to' list of government action and suits does not settle the boundary.
This definition is deleted and replaced twice, by Endorsement 8 and again by Endorsement 11, each adding a different limitation on covered 'claims'. Which text applies to a given loss is not stated.

Endorsement 10 deletes Definitions Subsection E. in its entirety and substitutes 'transportation', so this 'contingent transportation' definition no longer has a place in the instrument even though Exclusion VI.Q. as printed still refers to it. The two texts occupy the same lettered slot.

Definitions Subsection F. is 'deleted in its entirety and replaced' by both Endorsement 8 and Endorsement 11, which give materially different definitions of 'covered location' (blanket non-owned disposal sites in one, only scheduled ones in the other). Nothing in the instrument says which replacement controls.

The definition operates only if a 'Schedule of Insured Contracts Endorsement' is attached, and no such endorsement is among the sixteen attached at issuance. The carve-back in Exclusion VI.B. that depends on this definition is therefore empty.

'Environmental law' sweeps in any 'guidance document' and 'risk-based corrective action guidance', so non-binding material can define the scope of 'remediation costs ... required by environmental law'. Whether an agency guidance or directive 'governs the liability or responsibilities of the insured' is contestable.

The definition describes reporting a claim 'first made against the insured during or subsequent to the end of the policy period', which on its face extends the reporting mechanism to claims made after expiry, contrary to the claims-made preamble. The phrase is loose enough to support competing readings.

Endorsement 12 removes 'fungi' from the definition of 'pollution condition' and excludes fungi claims entirely, yet this definition and the fungi-specific machinery in 'certified industrial hygienist' and 'remediation costs' remain in force. The instrument retains apparatus for a risk it no longer insures.

'Illicit abandonment' lists specific substances and then a catch-all 'waste materials, including "low-level radioactive waste", "mixed waste" and medical, infectious and pathological wastes', so the reach of the general words against the enumerated specifics is uncertain. Whether infected carcasses or litter fall within the list is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

'Insured' sweeps in employees and officers of any insured, yet the Separation of Insureds condition operates only 'as if each "named insured" were the only "insured"'. The two provisions use different classes for the same purpose.

Endorsement 8 deletes this definition in its entirety and replaces it with a far narrower one (permitted, non-bankrupt, non-listed sites), and Endorsement 11 then re-uses the term differently. The instrument carries two competing meanings of 'non-owned disposal site'.

Paragraph 2. is grammatically broken — 'the period of time following the closing date ... or, as applicable, through the applicable expiration date' — so the start and end of the policy period for acquired locations cannot be read off the text. The defect changes what the defined term means.

The operative words are 'any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant, contaminant, or pollutant', followed by an illustrative list of industrial substances; whether a biological agent such as a virus or animal waste is an 'irritant, contaminant, or pollutant' is a classic and genuinely contested question. The general words sit against specific enumerated examples of a different character.

Endorsement 12 deletes this definition in its entirety, dropping 'fungi' and legionella and excluding odor, so the printed Subsection W. and the endorsed version state different scopes of the central insured risk. Which text governs is the threshold coverage question.

'Remediation costs' are limited to expenses incurred 'to the extent required by "environmental law"', a qualifier that leaves open whether voluntarily or commercially prudent response costs, or costs required by a non-environmental agency directive, are covered. The phrase does real coverage work and is capable of narrow and broad readings.

'Responsible person' turns on being an 'employee ... responsible for environmental affairs, control, or compliance', a description with no boundary in a multi-site farming operation. Knowledge of such a person triggers the Known Conditions and Intentional Non-Compliance exclusions.

The carve-back preserving coverage for 'environmental indemnity obligations' depends on a Schedule of Insured Contracts Endorsement that is not attached to this Policy, so the exception has nothing to operate on. The exclusion as applied is therefore broader than the exception suggests.

The closing list is misnumbered ('4. Whether an insured may be liable ...' followed by '2.'), a printing defect in a provision whose two limbs define the exclusion's reach. The error is mechanical but sits in the operative text.

The exclusion of 'any associated "claims" seeking exclusively injunctive relief in addition to such fines, penalties or damages' is self-contradictory: relief cannot be sought 'exclusively' and also 'in addition to' something else. The sentence cannot be applied as written.

The carve-back requires 'prior written approval of the Insurer at its sole discretion', while General Condition IX.M. provides that any consent required under the Policy 'shall not be unreasonably withheld, delayed, conditioned, or denied'. Sole discretion and a reasonableness constraint cannot both govern the same approval.

The bare exclusion of 'claims made by any insured against any other insured' operates against a definition of 'insured' that includes every employee, officer and additional insured, so it can bar ordinary third-party claims. Its intended reach is not stated.

The exclusion reaches anything 'related to' the 'intentional disregard of, or knowing, willful, or deliberate non-compliance with' any law, notice letter or 'instruction of any governmental agency', a list so broad that the required mental state and the causal link are both uncertain. 'Related to' has no boundary here.

The exclusion turns on conditions 'in existence and reported to a "responsible person"' without saying by whom, in what form, or with what specificity the report must be made. That undefined trigger controls a very large carve-out from Coverage B.

Both carve-backs depend on a 'Schedule of Known Conditions Endorsement attached to this Policy, if any', and no such schedule is among the endorsements attached at issuance. The exception cannot operate as the text contemplates.

The exclusion applies to a change in use or operations that 'materially increases the likelihood or severity' of a pollution condition compared with the uses 'identified' in the Application, with no benchmark for materiality. Both the comparison and the threshold are left to argument.

'Naturally occurring materials' is undefined, and the carve-back turns on whether the substance is present 'as a result of human activities or human processes' — a distinction that is genuinely contestable for biological or animal-derived matter at a farming site. Exclusion and exception can each be read to swallow the other.

Endorsement 8 deletes this exclusion in its entirety and replaces it with a differently structured 'Disposal Sites' exclusion, while the printed exception here refers to a Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement that is not attached. Two versions of the same lettered exclusion appear in the instrument.

The exclusion joins its opening condition to the numbered limbs with 'and' followed by limbs joined by 'or', leaving unclear whether both the knowledge requirement and one limb, or either limb alone, must be satisfied. It also refers to schedules that are not attached.

Endorsement 10 deletes Exclusion Q. in its entirety and replaces it with a version whose carve-back is for 'transportation', and it also deletes the definition of 'contingent transportation' on which this printed carve-back depends. The printed exception refers to a term that no longer exists.

Notice is required 'as soon as practicable' and the content requirements are stated in permissive terms ('Notice should include'), so neither the deadline nor the sufficiency of a notice can be fixed from the text. 'As soon as practicable' is the most litigated phrase in a notice condition.

This condition requires notice 'as soon as practicable', while the Declarations preamble and Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. make coverage conditional on written report 'during the policy period'. Whether a practicable-but-late report defeats coverage cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The list is misnumbered — items 3. and 4. lost their numerals and run into the preceding text — so the enumerated cooperation duties do not read cleanly. The defect is mechanical rather than substantive.

Endorsement 4, V.C. deletes this subsection in its entirety and replaces it with a version requiring only 'prior written consent' and extending to catastrophe management firms and costs. The printed 'prior express written consent' and the endorsed text differ in terms.

The insured must 'make every attempt to mitigate any loss' while the Insurer may step in if, 'in the sole judgment of the insurer', the insured fails to take reasonable steps; neither standard is measurable and the two use different tests. The consequence is that costs incurred by the Insurer are charged to the insured's retention.

The entitlement to an extended reporting period is tied to cancellation 'as described in Subsection A., Paragraph 1. of Section IX.' — the paragraph dealing only with cancellation by the first named insured — or nonrenewal, and says nothing about ordinary expiry or cancellation by the Insurer. The cross-reference makes the entitlement narrower than the rest of Section VIII. assumes.

Section VIII.A. limits the extended reporting period to cancellation and nonrenewal, while Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. and Section VIII.B. assume an 'extended reporting period' is available for claims reported after the policy period generally. The two cannot be squared for a policy that simply runs to expiry.

Endorsement 7 deletes this subsection and substitutes a ninety (90) day basic extended reporting period, so the instrument as printed states both sixty and ninety days. A reader must know the endorsement supersedes to reach the right number.

Endorsement 7 deletes this subsection and substitutes a thirty-three (33) month supplemental extended reporting period, so the document states both thirty-four and thirty-three months. The competing figures appear in the same instrument.

Paragraph 1. says the Policy 'may be cancelled only by the "first named insured"', while Paragraph 2. (and Endorsement 9) expressly permit cancellation by the Insurer for non-payment or misrepresentation. The word 'only' contradicts the very next paragraph.

The closing passage is self-cancelling: subparagraph 2.b. 'shall apply only to that insured that engages in the fraud', and then 'This exception shall not apply to any insured who is a parent corporation, subsidiary, employer of, or otherwise affiliated' — so it is unclear whether affiliates are protected or exposed. The double negative changes the meaning of the cancellation right.

Endorsement 9 deletes this paragraph in its entirety and substitutes a ninety-day notice, while Paragraph 1. of the same condition says the Policy may be cancelled 'only by the first named insured'. The instrument contains both the superseded sixty-day text and a flat contradiction of the Insurer's right.

This paragraph provides for pro rata earning and refund of 'unearned premium', while Item 5. of the Declarations deems the premium '100 % minimum-earned as of the first day of the Policy Period'. If the whole premium is minimum-earned there is never anything to refund under this condition.

The paragraph refers to 'the premium percentage identified in Item 5.' as the minimum-earned premium, but Item 5. states dollar amounts and a 100% figure, so the operative reference is imprecise. What is earned on cancellation cannot be computed from the words used.

Suit is barred 'unless all of the Policy terms have been fully complied with', a condition with no materiality or prejudice qualifier that would on its face defeat any action after any breach. Whether it means substantial compliance with conditions precedent is genuinely arguable.

The last sentence assumes 'other insurance to which this Policy is excess' and 'any underlying insurer', but the Policy is written as primary above a self-insured retention and the Other Insurance condition makes it excess only contingently. The excess premise sits oddly with the rest of the instrument.

Separation operates 'as if each "named insured" were the only "insured"', yet 'insured' is defined to include additional insureds, officers and employees who are not 'named insureds'. Whether those persons get the benefit of separation is not answered.

The clause makes this Policy excess over all other 'valid and collectible insurance' while excepting policies 'specifically written to apply in excess of this Policy', a formulation that collides with identically drafted clauses in other insurers' forms. Escape-and-excess clauses of this kind are routinely construed.

The clause requires submission to 'the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York' without naming a court, and is framed only around 'the failure of the Insurer to pay any amount claimed to be due', so whether it is a mandatory forum-selection clause and which disputes it captures are both open. It also refers to 'such court' when no court has been identified.

Endorsement 15 (Service of Suit) provides that 'If the insured requests, the company will submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction' and will accept that court's final decision, which cannot be squared with exclusive New York jurisdiction. The instrument gives the insured a choice of forum in one place and denies it in another.

The New York choice of law sits with the Jurisdiction and Venue condition and with Endorsement 15's promise to submit to 'any court of competent jurisdiction' and to accept that court's decision. Whether New York law travels with a suit brought elsewhere under the Service of Suit endorsement is a live question.

The no-waiver and no-change condition says the Policy may be changed only 'as provided by endorsement and attached to this Policy', yet several attached endorsements each purport to delete and replace the same subsections (Definitions F. and the Coverage A. grant). The rule for changes does not resolve which endorsement prevails.

This condition makes every consent subject to a reasonableness standard, but Exclusion VI.H. conditions its carve-back on approval 'at [the Insurer's] sole discretion' and Section VII.D. lets the Insurer act on its 'sole judgment'. The general condition and those specific grants of discretion cannot both stand.

Cover is given 'solely with respect to their vicarious liability arising out of any "named insured's" direct liability', a formulation whose scope (and the missing terminal punctuation) leaves the additional insured's protection uncertain. 'Vicarious liability' is not defined anywhere in the Policy.

The grant covers loss 'in excess of the Deductible Period', treating a period of days as if it were a monetary deductible, and requires reporting 'as soon as practicable, and during the "policy period"' — two different deadlines in one sentence. Both formulations are capable of competing readings.

The $5,000,000 business interruption sublimit is 'subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations', but the Total Policy Aggregate in Item 4. is only $7,000,000 and Coverage A's aggregate is $9,000,000. How the sublimit interacts with those inconsistent aggregates is unresolved.

'Business income' is defined to include 'Net profit or loss' and 'continuing operating and payroll expense', without saying how a loss figure is to be applied or over what measurement period. The measure of recovery cannot be derived from the definition alone.

'Necessary partial or complete suspension of the insured's operations' gives no test for when a slowdown becomes a 'suspension' or when a suspension is 'necessary'. In a partial-shutdown loss that word does all the work.

Business interruption cover is confined to a pollution condition 'for which coverage is otherwise afforded ... for "remediation costs" resulting from the first-party discovery of such "pollution condition"', a compound and opaque qualifier that decides whether any business interruption loss is payable at all. Whether a condition that generates third-party claims but no covered remediation costs qualifies is genuinely arguable.

The definition confines cover to conditions 'on, at or under a "covered location"', omitting the 'migrating from' limb that Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. include. The endorsement's scope is narrower than the coverage it says it tracks.

The period ends when the condition 'has been remedied to the point at which the insured's normal operations could reasonably be restored', and coverage is then denied for loss caused by 'unfavorable business conditions caused by the impact of the covered pollution condition'. Separating recovery-period loss from excluded market impact is an inherently contestable line.

The appraisal machinery is permissive ('either may make written demand') yet the resulting decision 'shall be binding upon both parties', while the Insurer 'shall still retain all of its rights ... to deny all or a portion of the claim'. Whether appraisal is a condition precedent and what a 'binding' award settles are both open.

The exclusion refers to 'any of the individually excluded exposures identified above' without identifying anything above it in the endorsement, so its referent must be supplied from outside the sentence. As written it excludes nothing identifiable.

A catastrophe-management-specific retention of $100,000 is stated here, while the coverage grant in the same endorsement speaks of costs 'in excess of the "self-insured retention"', a term defined in Section V.AA. by reference to Items 2.d. and 3.d. Whether one or two retentions must be paid for a single event is not resolved.

The grant applies to costs 'in excess of the "self-insured retention"' as defined in Section V.AA., while the same endorsement sets a separate Catastrophe Management-Specific Self-Insured Retention. Which retention applies to catastrophe management costs is left unstated.

'Adverse media coverage' requires 'national or regional news exposure' that is 'reasonably likely to have a negative impact' on reputation, community relations or good will, none of which is measurable. The trigger for the whole supplemental coverage rests on that phrase.

The event is defined by 'the good faith opinion of a "key executive"' that claims will exceed the retention and that services will be needed, making a subjective opinion the coverage trigger. Whether the opinion was held in good faith and whether it must be objectively reasonable are both open.

The enumerated categories close with 'other necessary response costs', a general catch-all appended to a specific list of medical, funeral, counselling, travel and temporary living costs. How far the catch-all extends beyond the enumerated kinds is the classic ejusdem generis question.

The exclusion bites on 'any of the individually excluded exposures identified above', but nothing above it in the endorsement identifies excluded exposures. The referent must be imported from Section VI. of the Policy, and the sentence does not say so.

Several of the scheduled Retroactive Dates are mistyped — '11/01/2074', '41/01/2014' and '11/07/2014' — and those dates fix the earliest date from which a pollution condition at those sites is covered. The error goes directly to the scope of Coverage A at six locations.

This endorsement deletes and replaces Insuring Agreement I.A. in its entirety, and Endorsement 10 then deletes and replaces the same Subsection A. with a transportation version that omits the retroactive-date limb. Which replacement governs Coverage A for the six retroactive-dated sites is unanswered.

The replacement per-condition limit covers only 'claims' and 'remediation costs' and drops 'legal defense expense', while the Declarations preamble states that legal defense expenses erode the Limits of Liability. The endorsement's Subsection D. and Section III.D. as replaced handle defense costs differently again.

Item 2.c.'s $9,000,000 aggregate is again called 'the maximum liability of the Insurer pursuant to this Policy', although Item 4.'s Total Policy Aggregate is $7,000,000 and Section II.G. gives it the same status. The replacement text reproduces the inconsistency rather than curing it.

The replacement limits Coverage B to conditions 'resulting from "covered operations"', a quoted term that is defined nowhere in the Policy or its endorsements. A quoted term with no definition cannot be applied as written.

By confining the Coverage B per-condition limit to conditions 'resulting from "covered operations"', this text imposes a restriction absent from Insuring Agreement I.B., which covers any pollution condition on, at, under or migrating from a covered location. The limit and the grant do not describe the same risk.

The Coverage B aggregate is tied to 'all "pollution conditions" resulting from "covered operations"', but 'covered operations' is a quoted term that appears nowhere in the definitions. The aggregate cannot be applied without supplying a meaning the instrument does not give.

This aggregate covers only conditions 'resulting from "covered operations"', a qualifier absent from Insuring Agreement I.B. and from Section II.F. as originally printed. The scope of the aggregate and the scope of the grant diverge.

The replacement defence duty ends on exhaustion of 'any applicable Aggregate Limit or Sublimit of Liability', which read literally would end the duty when a $250,000 catastrophe management or $500,000 natural resource damage sublimit is exhausted. That cannot be reconciled with the continuing coverage those endorsements provide.

Defence costs are said to reduce only the Dedicated Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate, while Section III.D. as printed says they reduce the limits in Items 2., 3. and 4. and the Declarations preamble says they erode 'THE LIMITS OF LIABILITY'. The erosion rules in the instrument do not match.

The settlement sentence is corrupt — 'If the insurer recommends a settlement of any ongoing or future "claim" for which it is not which is acceptable to a claimant' — and the paragraph then caps liability for covered 'loss', a term the Policy never defines. Both defects sit in the operative words that fix the Insurer's exposure.

This ninety-day basic extended reporting period replaces the sixty-day period in Section VIII.C., which remains printed in the policy form. The instrument states two different figures for the same period.

The thirty-three month supplemental period replaces the thirty-four months stated in Section VIII.D., which remains printed. The two figures for the same optional extension appear in the same document.

Endorsement 8 deletes Definitions Subsection F. and makes any 'non-owned disposal site' a covered location, while Endorsement 11 deletes the same Subsection F. and limits that limb to sites 'identified in the Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement'. Two attached endorsements give the same defined term incompatible scopes.

Limb 3. cross-refers to 'third-party "claims" pursuant to Subsection D., above', but Subsection D. appears after this text in the endorsement, so the internal cross-reference does not point where it says. The reader cannot locate the limitation from the words used.

The replacement restricts covered claims to waste 'received at the "non-owned disposal site"' during the policy period or after a 1 November 2003 Retroactive Date, while Endorsement 11 deletes and replaces the same Subsection D. with a wholly different limitation for non-owned covered locations. Two attached endorsements occupy the same definitional slot.

Qualification depends on the site having been 'properly permitted and licensed' and not 'undergoing voluntary or regulatory-required remediation activities' at the time of disposal — historical facts about third parties that the insured cannot verify and that admit of degree. Each of the four conditions is a potential coverage fight.

Limb 2. excludes conditions at non-owned disposal sites that received waste before 'any Retroactive Date identified in Section V., DEFINITIONS, Subsection D.', but Endorsement 11 deletes and replaces that same Subsection D. and contains no retroactive date. The cross-reference may point to text that no longer exists.

The closing passage says subparagraph 2.b. applies 'only to that insured that engages in the fraud' and then that 'This exception shall not apply to any insured who is a parent corporation, subsidiary, employer of, or otherwise affiliated by ownership', leaving affiliates' position self-contradictory. The double negative changes who can be cancelled.

The Insurer's cancellation right stated here is flatly contradicted by Section IX.A.1., which says the Policy 'may be cancelled only by the "first named insured"'. Endorsement 9 replaces Paragraph 2. but leaves Paragraph 1.'s 'only' untouched.

This 'all other terms remain unchanged' saving clause appears in every endorsement, including several that delete and replace the same subsections as one another (Definitions F. and Insuring Agreement A.). It provides no rule for resolving the resulting conflicts.

Endorsement 10 deletes and replaces Insuring Agreement I.A. in its entirety and, unlike Endorsement 5's replacement of the same subsection, restores the requirement that conditions 'first commence, in their entirety, during the "policy period"' with no retroactive-date limb. If this text governs it silently withdraws the retroactive cover Endorsement 5 gave six scheduled locations.

This definition occupies Definitions Subsection E., which previously defined 'contingent transportation', a term still relied on by Exclusion VI.Q. as printed in the policy form. The replacement leaves the printed exclusion pointing at a defunct term.

Endorsement 11 deletes Definitions Subsection F. and replaces it, but Endorsement 8 does exactly the same with a materially wider limb 3. (any non-owned disposal site, not only scheduled ones). Two endorsements attached at issuance give the central term 'covered location' different meanings.

Limb 3. refers to sites 'identified in the Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement attached to this Policy', and no such schedule is attached, so that limb has no content. Limb 4. then adds 'non-owned covered location' as a species of covered location without saying whether the Policy's location-based limits apply to them.

Claims for non-owned covered locations exclude any claim 'from or made in relation to the owner, operator, contractor of the "non-owned covered location": or those of their employees' — an unpunctuated list with no conjunction and the open-ended phrase 'in relation to'. Whether a claim by a contract grower or its insurer is excluded turns on words that cannot be parsed with confidence.

This replacement of Definitions Subsection D. requires only that the claim be 'first made during the "policy period"', dropping the written-reporting condition that Endorsement 8's competing replacement of the same subsection and the claims-made preamble both impose. The two replacements of Subsection D. cannot both apply.

The sites qualify only if, 'pursuant to an agreement with the insured', they 'produce certain egg related products on behalf of the insured' — 'certain' identifies nothing and 'egg related products' has no boundary. Whether a scheduled grower that has changed its arrangement still qualifies turns on those words.

'Non-owned covered locations' are defined as sites 'not owned or operated by any insured', yet Endorsement 11's amended 'covered location' definition brings them in as covered locations, and Exclusion VI.C. (Divested Property) and the Coverage Territory condition are drafted for owned sites. The category does not sit comfortably in the rest of the instrument.

The definition turns on 'the discharge, dispersal, release, escape, migration or seepage of any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant, contaminant, or pollutant', illustrated only by industrial substances, so whether a biological agent such as an avian virus or infected manure is within it is genuinely contestable. The general words and the enumerated specifics pull in different directions.

This endorsement deletes the printed Subsection W., removing 'fungi' and legionella from the insured risk, yet the Policy retains the 'fungi' definition, the 'certified industrial hygienist' definition and the fungi limb of 'remediation costs'. The instrument still contains machinery for a risk this text removes.

The exclusion adds 'odor' alongside fungi and legionella, but Endorsement 12's own replacement definition of 'pollution condition' already says the term 'does not include any odor'. The same endorsement removes odor from the grant and then excludes it, leaving the exclusion's independent work unclear.

The $500,000 natural resource damage sublimit is 'subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations', where Item 2.c. ($9,000,000) and Item 4. ($7,000,000) already conflict. It also caps only 'claims' and defence expenses, saying nothing about remediation costs for the same damage.

The retroactive limb reads 'on or after the on or after the Retroactive Date, if any', a duplicated phrase in the words that fix the earliest covered product pollution. The provision also grants cover for claims 'first made during the "policy period"' without the discovery machinery used elsewhere.

The sublimit is said to cap 'all "claims", "remediation costs" and associated "legal defense expense"' arising out of product pollution, although the coverage grant in the same endorsement insures only 'claims' and associated defence expense and not remediation costs. The limit and the grant describe different heads of loss.

The new exclusion removes all claims 'arising out of any goods or products manufactured, sold or distributed by an insured' — for an egg producer, nearly everything — subject only to a carve-back for 'product pollution'. The width of 'arising out of any goods or products' against the narrow carve-back is a real construction problem.

This exclusion is added to Section VI. after the Policy has already granted Coverage A. and B. for pollution conditions at covered locations, and it would on its face defeat claims arising from product handling at those locations. Reconciling it with Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. requires more than the carve-back supplies.

'Product Pollution' requires that the use of the product occur 'after the insured has relinquished possession', and the sentence is broken by an interpolated page footer, ending with a carve-out that 'products do not include waste products'. Where possession ends, and the line between product and waste, are both left to argument.

The promise to enter a general appearance in 'any action, suit or proceeding instituted against the company' is difficult to square with General Condition IX.I., which requires the parties to submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of New York. The two provisions address the same subject from opposite directions.

The company's promise to 'submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction' at the insured's request cannot be reconciled with General Condition IX.I., which makes New York jurisdiction 'exclusive'. Whether the service of suit endorsement waives or merely supplements the forum clause is the classic dispute over this pairing.

'Submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction' may mean only a consent to personal jurisdiction and service, or a consent to the insured's choice of venue; the sentence does not say which. That single phrase decides where suit may be brought.

The promise to 'accept the final decision of that court' reinforces the insured's forum choice under the Service of Suit endorsement and pulls against the exclusive New York jurisdiction required by General Condition IX.I. Read with the preceding sentence it is the strongest textual answer to that clause.

The Canadian service-of-suit provision assumes an insured resident in Canada, while Section IV. limits coverage to pollution conditions located and claims made 'within the United States of America'. The endorsement contemplates a situation the coverage territory excludes.

The saving clause preserves the Policy's terms 'OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED', so whether the preceding submission to 'any court of competent jurisdiction' is one of the things 'above stated' that does vary General Condition IX.I. is precisely what the sentence leaves open. It is the pivot on which the forum dispute turns.

The phrase 'OTHER THAN AS ABOVE STATED' does not identify which of the preceding sentences are intended to vary the Policy, so the exception swallows or preserves the clause depending on the reading chosen. The words alone cannot fix the scope of the carve-out.
